intro: CPA (cost per acquisition) shows what one conversion actually cost a specific channel or campaign — a lead, a trial, or a sale, depending on what's being tracked. Enter total spend and conversions to see the rate.

sections.heading: How CPA is calculated
sections.body: CPA = Total Spend ÷ Conversions — [the same total-spend-over-conversions shape Geckoboard uses to define Cost Per Acquisition](https://www.geckoboard.com/resources/kpi-examples/cost-per-acquisition-cpa/), applied to a specific channel or campaign rather than the whole business, downstream of what [CPC](/calculators/cpc) already measured for the clicks that led to those conversions. What counts as a "conversion" isn't fixed by the formula itself — it's whatever action the spend was actually paying for, and that choice changes what the resulting number means.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body: $4,000 ÷ 80 = $50.00 per conversion. Whether that's a good number depends entirely on what "conversion" was set to mean here — $50 per qualified sale reads very differently than $50 per newsletter signup.

sections.heading: CPA depends on which conversion you're counting
sections.body: The formula never specifies what a conversion is — a lead, a trial signup, a form fill, or a completed sale can all be plugged into the same denominator, and each produces a technically correct but very different CPA. A campaign optimizing for form fills will show a low CPA that says nothing about how many of those leads ever became paying customers. That's not a flaw in the metric; it's why the conversion definition needs to be stated next to the number every time it's reported, rather than assumed to mean the same thing across campaigns, teams, or reporting periods.

sections.heading: CPA vs. CAC
sections.body: Both answer a "what did it cost to get one" question, but at different scopes. [CPA](https://www.geckoboard.com/resources/kpi-examples/cost-per-acquisition-cpa/) applies to a specific channel or campaign, using whatever conversion event that channel is being measured against — a lead, a trial, or a sale. [CAC](/calculators/cac) is a company-wide average across every acquisition channel and the overhead behind them (sales salaries, tools, and other costs beyond media spend), divided specifically by new paying customers. A campaign can post a low CPA on cheap leads while the company's overall CAC stays high, because CPA never had to account for what happened to those leads afterward, or for any cost beyond that one channel's spend.

faq.a: CPA (cost per acquisition) is the average amount spent to generate one conversion from a specific marketing channel or campaign, calculated as total spend divided by the number of conversions. Unlike a company-wide metric, CPA is meant to be read at the channel or campaign level — a paid search campaign's CPA, a specific ad set's CPA — rather than as a single blended figure across every acquisition source. What counts as a "conversion" is set by whoever is running the campaign: it might be a completed sale, a trial signup, or a qualified lead, and that choice is what actually determines what the resulting CPA number means.

Divide total spend by the number of conversions: CPA = Total Spend ÷ Conversions. A campaign that spent $4,000 and generated 80 conversions has a CPA of $4,000 ÷ 80 = $50.00. Both numbers need to describe the same channel, campaign, and time period — spend from a full month divided by conversions counted over only part of it produces a CPA that doesn't accurately describe either period. The conversion definition also needs to stay fixed between calculations: comparing a CPA computed against leads with one computed against completed sales isn't a real comparison, even if both are labeled "CPA."

faq.q: Is CPA the same as CAC?
faq.a: No, though they're often used loosely as if they were. CPA is scoped to a specific channel or campaign and can be measured against any conversion event that channel is optimizing for — a lead, a trial, or a sale. CAC is a company-wide average, typically covering every acquisition channel plus the sales and marketing overhead behind them (salaries, tools, and other costs beyond media spend), divided specifically by new paying customers acquired. A single channel's CPA on cheap leads can look great while the company's overall CAC stays high, because CPA never has to account for what happens to those leads downstream, or for costs outside that one channel.

There's no universal good CPA — it depends on the conversion definition being used, the industry, the channel, and what a single conversion is actually worth to the business, all of which shift the number for reasons unrelated to campaign quality. A $50 CPA on qualified sales in a high-ticket B2B business can be excellent, while the same $50 CPA on a low-value lead in a different business can be a loss. Rather than comparing against an outside benchmark, CPA is most useful measured against what a conversion at that definition is actually worth, or tracked over time within the same campaign and conversion definition.
